column4: Develop and use a model to illustrate the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within multicellular organisms.
Identify the levels of biological organization in multicellular organisms (cells, tissues, organs, organ systems, organism). [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can name the levels of organization in an organism, from cells to the whole organism.

column4: Recognize that all living things are made of cells, the basic unit of structure and function. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can state that all living things are made of cells, the basic unit of structure and function.

column4: Describe how each level is composed of the level below it (cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems). [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can describe how each level is built from the level below it.

column4: Explain how the structure at each level relates to the specific function it performs, and how systems interact to keep the organism functioning. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can explain how a part's structure fits its job, and how an organism's systems work together.

column4: Use a model or diagram to illustrate how interacting systems work together to carry out a specific function (e.g., nutrient uptake, water delivery, movement in response to stimuli). [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can use a model to show how an organism's systems work together to do one job, like moving.

column4: Develop a model that illustrates the hierarchical organization of interacting systems that provide specific functions within a multicellular organism. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can build my own model showing how levels and systems in an organism work together to carry out functions.

column4: Taught in Unit 1.1: Organization in Organisms (CP: Cells to Organisms).

Describe how a negative feedback loop (stimulus, response) keeps a body condition within a steady range, and how positive feedback differs by pushing a change further. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can describe how negative feedback keeps a body condition steady and how positive feedback differs.

column4: Use data from an investigation, such as heart rate before and after exercise, as evidence that a feedback mechanism returns a condition toward normal. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can use data, like heart rate after exercise, to show feedback bringing the body back to normal.

column4: Plan and conduct an investigation to provide evidence that feedback mechanisms maintain homeostasis. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can carry out an investigation that shows feedback keeping the body in balance.

column4: Taught in Unit 1.1: Organization in Organisms (CP: Cells to Organisms).
Describe that cell division (mitosis) makes new cells with the same DNA, for growth and repair. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can describe how cell division makes new cells with the same DNA, for growth and repair.

column4: Explain that cells with the same DNA become specialized (differentiation) by using different genes, and so form different tissues, without the mechanisms of gene control. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can explain that cells with the same DNA specialize by using different genes.

column4: Use a model to illustrate the role of cellular division (mitosis) and differentiation in producing and maintaining complex organisms. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.1]
column5: I can use a model to show how cell division and specialization build and maintain a body.

column4: Develop a model to illustrate the role of photosynthesis and cellular respiration in the cycling of carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere.

Identify the four spheres and where carbon is stored in each: carbon dioxide in air, dissolved carbon in water, living and dead matter, and rock and fossil fuels. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can name the four spheres and where carbon is stored in each one.

column4: Name the processes besides photosynthesis and respiration that move carbon between spheres: burning, dissolving into and out of the ocean, burial into rock and fossil fuels, and volcanic release. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can name processes besides photosynthesis and respiration that move carbon, like burning and burial in rock.

column4: Describe photosynthesis as moving carbon from the atmosphere and hydrosphere into the biosphere, and cellular respiration as moving it back. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can describe how photosynthesis moves carbon from air and water into living things, and respiration moves it back.

column4: Use a carbon-cycle model to trace a carbon atom through at least three spheres, naming the process at each transfer. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can trace one carbon atom through at least three spheres and name each process that moves it.

column4: Use a model or simulation to predict how a change in one flow, such as burning fossil fuels or clearing forest, changes the carbon stored in other spheres. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can use a model to predict what happens to carbon elsewhere when one part of the cycle changes.

column4: Develop a model to illustrate the role of photosynthesis and cellular respiration in the cycling of carbon among the biosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere, and geosphere. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can build a model showing how photosynthesis and respiration cycle carbon among all four spheres.

column4: Taught in Unit 1.2: Energy Through Carbon.
Name the inputs (carbon dioxide, water, light) and outputs (sugar, oxygen) of photosynthesis. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can name what photosynthesis uses and what it makes.

column4: Explain that photosynthesis transforms light energy into chemical energy stored in sugar and oxygen, which respiration later releases. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can explain how photosynthesis stores light energy as chemical energy in sugar.

column4: Use a model to illustrate how photosynthesis transforms light energy into stored chemical energy, tracking the matter that goes in and comes out. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can use a model to show photosynthesis storing light energy in sugar, and track the matter in and out.

column4: Taught in Unit 1.2: Energy Through Carbon.
Name the inputs (sugar, oxygen) and outputs (carbon dioxide, water, usable energy) of cellular respiration. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can name what cellular respiration uses and what it makes.

column4: Explain that cellular respiration breaks the bonds in food and oxygen molecules and forms bonds in new compounds, with a net release of energy the cell can use. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can explain how respiration breaks and forms bonds, releasing energy a cell can use.

column4: Use a model to illustrate that cellular respiration is a chemical process in which bonds are broken and new bonds formed, resulting in a net transfer of energy. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.2]
column5: I can use a model to show respiration breaking and forming bonds, releasing more energy than it uses.

column4: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules may combine with other elements to form amino acids and/or other large carbon-based molecules.

Identify that sugar molecules and large carbon-based molecules (amino acids, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids) are composed largely of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can name the three elements that make up most of sugar and the body's large molecules.

column4: Describe how organisms take in matter (for growth and maintenance) and rearrange atoms through chemical reactions, with matter conserved. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can describe how living things take in matter and rearrange its atoms, with no atoms lost.

column4: Explain that chemical reactions rearrange atoms from simpler reactants into more complex products, sometimes incorporating other elements (e.g., nitrogen, sulfur). [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can explain how atoms from sugar join with other elements, like nitrogen, to build larger molecules.

column4: Use a model or simulation to trace atoms from sugar molecules as they recombine with other elements to form amino acids and other macromolecules. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can use a model to trace atoms from sugar into a larger molecule.

column4: Construct an explanation, based on evidence, for how carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen from sugar molecules combine with other elements to form large carbon-based molecules. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can use evidence to explain how atoms from sugar combine with other elements to build large carbon-based molecules.

column4: Revise the explanation in light of new evidence from models, simulations, students' own investigations, or peer review. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can revise my explanation when new evidence comes in.

column4: Taught in Unit 1.3: Sugar to Structures.
Count the atoms of each element on each side of a simple chemical reaction. [DOK 1; Thread (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can count the atoms of each element on both sides of a reaction.

column4: Explain that a chemical reaction rearranges atoms, so the number of each kind of atom, and so the mass, stays the same. [DOK 2; Thread (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can explain why a reaction keeps every atom, so the total mass stays the same.

column4: Use atom counts to support the claim that atoms, and therefore mass, are conserved when sugar is rebuilt into larger molecules, using a simple reaction such as two sugars joining and releasing water. [DOK 2; Thread (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can use atom counts to show that no atoms are lost when sugar is rebuilt.

column4: Taught in Unit 1.3: Sugar to Structures.

Identify the criteria a solution must meet and the constraints it must work within, such as cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, and its possible social, cultural, and environmental impacts. [DOK 1; Thread (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can list what a solution must do, the limits it must work within, and its possible impacts.

column4: Compare the trade-offs of two solutions to the same problem using given data. [DOK 2; Thread (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can use data to compare what two solutions gain and give up.

column4: Evaluate a solution to a complex real-world problem, such as algae biofuel, based on prioritized criteria and trade-offs. [DOK 3; Thread (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 1.3]
column5: I can judge a real solution, like algae fuel, by ranking what matters and weighing gains against costs.

column4: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the structure of DNA determines the structure of proteins, which carry out the essential functions of life through systems of specialized cells.
Students can label or describe DNA as a double helix made of nucleotides containing sugar, phosphate, and nitrogen bases. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can describe DNA as a double helix built from nucleotides, each with a sugar, a phosphate, and a base.

column4: Students can state that DNA contains the genetic instructions for building proteins. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can state that DNA holds the instructions for building proteins.

column4: Students can describe the role of mRNA and tRNA in the transcription and translation processes. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can describe how a gene's message is copied and read to build a chain of amino acids.

column4: Students can explain that a single base change can alter a protein and possibly change its function. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can explain how changing one DNA base can change a protein and what it does.

column4: Students connect the idea that DNA codes for proteins and that these proteins contribute to the specialized functions of different cells [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can explain how DNA, through proteins, gives different cells their different jobs.

column4: Students use data from case studies or simulations to analyze the impacts of protein defects (e.g., sickle cell anemia or cystic fibrosis). [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can use case data, like sickle cell, to explain how a DNA change affects the body.

column4: Taught in Unit 2.1: DNA to Proteins.

Describe a chromosome as one long DNA molecule packed with proteins, and a gene as a section of that DNA that codes for a protein that affects a trait. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can describe how chromosomes, DNA, and genes are related.

column4: Explain how offspring receive one set of chromosomes, and so genes, from each parent. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can explain how a child gets half of its chromosomes from each parent.

column4: Ask questions to clarify relationships about the role of DNA and chromosomes in coding the instructions for characteristic traits passed from parents to offspring. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 2.1]
column5: I can ask questions that clarify how DNA and chromosomes carry the instructions for traits passed to offspring.

column4: Make and defend a claim based on evidence that inheritable genetic variations may result from (1) new genetic combinations through meiosis, (2) viable errors occurring during replication, and/or (3) mutations caused by environmental factors.

Name three sources of inheritable genetic variation: new gene combinations through meiosis, errors in DNA copying, and mutations caused by environmental factors. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can name three ways new genetic variation arises.

column4: Describe how meiosis and fertilization give offspring new combinations of alleles, without naming the phases of meiosis. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can describe how making sex cells and fertilization mix alleles into new combinations.

column4: Explain how a viable error in DNA copying, or a mutation caused by an environmental factor such as UV light, can change a gene, and why, in animals, only changes in cells that make eggs or sperm are inherited. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can explain how copying errors and things like UV light change genes, and when that change is inherited.

column4: Interpret data, such as mutation counts under different exposures or trait combinations in offspring, as evidence for a source of variation. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can read data as evidence for where a genetic variation came from.

column4: Make a claim, supported by data, about which source or sources explain a given case of inheritable genetic variation. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can make a claim, backed by data, about what caused a genetic variation.

column4: Defend the claim against a counterclaim or new data, explaining why the evidence supports one source over another. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can defend my claim against another explanation using the evidence.

column4: Taught in Unit 2.2: Inherited Instructions.
Use a Punnett square to list the possible allele combinations from a cross. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can use a Punnett square to show the possible allele combinations from a cross.

column4: Calculate the probability of each trait among offspring as a fraction or percent, and compare it with observed counts. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can calculate the chance of each trait and compare it with real counts.

column4: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to explain the variation and distribution of expressed traits in a population, including the role of environmental factors. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 2.2]
column5: I can use probability to explain how traits vary and spread in a population, including effects of environment.

column4: Evaluate evidence of the past and current movements of continental and oceanic crust and the theory of plate tectonics to explain the ages of crustal rocks.
Describe Earth's outer layer (lithosphere) as moving plates that carry continental or oceanic crust, and name the three kinds of plate boundary. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can describe Earth's outer layer as moving plates and name three kinds of plate boundaries.

column4: Describe how new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and is destroyed at subduction zones. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can describe where ocean crust is made and where it sinks back down.

column4: Read a map or graph of rock ages and describe the pattern: oceanic crust is older farther from a ridge, and continental crust is oldest near an ancient core. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can read a rock-age map and describe the pattern in the ages.

column4: Explain why oceanic crust is young compared with the oldest continental rocks, and why continental crust is youngest far from its ancient core, using how each kind of crust forms, grows, and is recycled. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can explain why ocean crust is young and why continents are oldest at their ancient cores.

column4: Evaluate evidence, such as rock ages, magnetic striping, and measured plate motion, for past and current movements of continental and oceanic crust. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can judge how strong the evidence is that the crust has moved and is still moving.

column4: Evaluate how well the theory of plate tectonics explains the ages of crustal rocks, using evidence from both oceanic and continental crust. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can judge how well plate tectonics explains the ages of rocks, using evidence.

column4: Taught in Unit 3.1: Age of the Earth.

Describe the evidence for Earth's early history: radiometric ages of meteorites, moon rocks, and Earth's oldest minerals, and the impact-crater record. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can list the evidence scientists use to learn about early Earth.

column4: Explain why the age of the solar system, about 4.6 billion years, comes mostly from meteorites and moon rocks rather than from Earth's own rocks. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can explain why meteorites and moon rocks tell Earth's age better than Earth rocks do.

column4: Apply scientific reasoning and evidence from ancient Earth materials, meteorites, and other planetary surfaces to construct an account of Earth's formation and early history. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.1]
column5: I can use evidence from rocks, meteorites, and other planets to tell how Earth formed.

column4: Construct an argument based on evidence about the simultaneous coevolution of Earth's systems and life on Earth.

Identifies examples of changes in Earth systems (e.g., volcanic eruptions, plate movement, climate shifts) and life on Earth (e.g., species changes, extinctions), but does not yet connect them. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.2]
column5: I can name examples of how Earth has changed and how life has changed.

column4: Describes basic interactions between Earth's systems and living organisms (e.g., photosynthesis increasing oxygen levels, or how volcanic eruptions impact species). Begins to relate cause and effect. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.2]
column5: I can describe one way Earth changed life and one way life changed Earth.

column4: Explains how specific events in Earth's history (e.g., ice ages, mass extinctions, oxygenation events) influenced the evolution of life and vice versa. Demonstrates understanding of reciprocal change. [DOK 2/3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.2]
column5: I can explain how events in Earth's history changed life, and how life in turn changed Earth.

column4: Constructs a logical argument using specific evidence from geoscience and biological records to show how life and Earth systems influenced each other. Organizes claim, reasoning, and supporting data. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.2]
column5: I can write an argument, with evidence, that Earth and life changed each other.

column4: Evaluates multiple lines of evidence (e.g., fossil records, geologic data, atmospheric composition) to synthesize a coherent argument. Considers feedback loops, time scales, and long-term interactions in constructing a persuasive scientific explanation. [DOK 4; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.2]
column5: I can combine several kinds of evidence into one strong argument about Earth and life.

column4: Construct an argument based on evidence about the simultaneous coevolution of Earth's systems and life on Earth. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.2]
column5: I can argue from evidence that Earth's systems and life have changed together over time.

column4: Communicate scientific information that common ancestry and biological evolution are supported by multiple lines of empirical evidence.
Describe what I already know and wonder about how different animals and humans are connected over time. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.3]
column5: I can say what I already know and wonder about how living things are related.

column4: Understand what types of evidence prove common ancestry [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.3]
column5: I can describe the kinds of evidence that support common ancestry: DNA, body structures, and embryos.

column4: Communicate how common ancestry is supported by evidence [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.3]
column5: I can explain to others how several lines of evidence support common ancestry.

column4: Understand what types of evidence prove biological evolution [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.3]
column5: I can describe the kinds of evidence that support evolution, like the fossil record.

column4: Communicate how biological evolution is supported by evidence. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.3]
column5: I can explain to others how several lines of evidence support evolution.

column4: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptation of populations.
Vocabulary: natural selection, adaptation, populations, abiotic, biotic [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can define natural selection, adaptation, population, biotic, and abiotic.

column4: Understanding the connection between natural selection and evolution [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can describe how natural selection causes a population to evolve.

column4: Evaluating evidence of natural selection as part of evolution [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can use data to show that a population's traits shifted because of natural selection.

column4: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how natural selection leads to adaptations of populations. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can use evidence to explain how natural selection makes a population better suited to its environment.

column4: Taught in Unit 3.4: Evolution by Selection.

Name the four factors: potential to increase in number, heritable variation from mutation and sexual reproduction, competition for limited resources, and greater survival and reproduction of better-suited organisms. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can name the four factors that drive evolution.

column4: Describe the influence of each factor on a population, using simple distribution graphs and proportional reasoning. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can use simple graphs to describe how each factor affects a population.

column4: Construct an explanation based on evidence that the process of evolution primarily results from the four factors. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can use evidence to explain how the four factors together cause evolution.

column4: Taught in Unit 3.4: Evolution by Selection.
Read a graph or table showing the proportion of a trait in a population across generations. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can read a graph that shows how common a trait is over several generations.

column4: Calculate the percent of a population with a trait in each generation and describe the trend. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can calculate the percent with a trait in each generation and describe the trend.

column4: Apply concepts of statistics and probability to support explanations that organisms with an advantageous heritable trait tend to increase in proportion to organisms lacking this trait. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can use statistics to show that a helpful inherited trait becomes more common.

column4: Taught in Unit 3.4: Evolution by Selection.
Distinguish group behavior from individual behavior, with examples such as flocking, schooling, and cooperative hunting. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can tell group behavior from individual behavior and give examples.

column4: Identify evidence of an outcome of a group behavior, such as survival or feeding success, in a data set. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can find evidence in data of what a group behavior does for survival.

column4: Evaluate evidence for the role of group behavior on individual and species' chances to survive and reproduce. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 3.4]
column5: I can judge evidence about how group behavior affects an animal's chances to survive and reproduce.

column4: Use mathematical representations to support claims for the cycling of matter and flow of energy among organisms in an ecosystem.
Identify Basic Components of an Ecosystem [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can name producers, consumers, and decomposers and the role of each.

column4: Describe the Movement of Matter and Energy [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can describe how matter cycles and energy flows through a food web.

column4: Interpret Visual and Mathematical Models of Energy and Matter [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can interpret energy pyramids and matter diagrams, including the 10 percent rule.

column4: Use Quantitative Data to Describe Energy Flow [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can use numbers to show how much energy passes from one level to the next.

column4: Use Quantitative Data to Describe Matter Cycling [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can use numbers to show that matter is conserved as it cycles.

column4: Construct Claims Supported by Mathematical Representations [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can use math to support a claim about how matter cycles and energy flows.

column4: Taught in Unit 4.1: Cycles of Life.
Describe aerobic respiration (with oxygen) and anaerobic respiration (without oxygen) by their inputs and outputs. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can compare what goes in and out of respiration with and without oxygen.

column4: Explain how matter cycles and energy flows where oxygen is present and where it is scarce, such as waterlogged soil or working muscle, and why less energy is released where oxygen is scarce. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can explain how matter and energy move where oxygen is plentiful and where it is scarce.

column4: Construct and revise an explanation based on evidence for the cycling of matter and flow of energy in aerobic and anaerobic conditions. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can explain, and revise with new evidence, how matter and energy move with and without oxygen.

column4: Taught in Unit 4.1: Cycles of Life.

Describe what a climate record, such as atmospheric carbon dioxide, temperature, sea level, or ice volume, shows about change over time. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can describe what a climate record shows about change over time.

column4: Determine the current rate of one climate change from a graph of geoscience data, such as degrees per decade or millimeters of sea level per year. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can find how fast one part of climate is changing from a graph.

column4: Analyze geoscience data and the results from global climate models to make an evidence-based forecast of one climate change and its future impacts on Earth's systems. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.1]
column5: I can use data and climate models to forecast one climate change and its effects.

column4: Use mathematical representations to support and revise explanations based on evidence about factors affecting biodiversity and populations in ecosystems of different scales.

Define population and biodiversity, and identify factors that affect them in an ecosystem (resources, predation, competition, disease, climate, available space). [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can define population and biodiversity and name factors that change them.

column4: Read and interpret graphs, charts, and data tables showing population sizes or biodiversity over time or across locations. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can read graphs and tables of population or biodiversity data.

column4: Determine mathematical patterns from data (e.g., averages, rates of change, trends) for populations or biodiversity. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can find averages, rates of change, and trends in population data.

column4: Compare populations and biodiversity within and across ecosystems of different scales using mathematical representations. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can use math to compare populations and biodiversity across ecosystems of different sizes.

column4: Use mathematical representations as evidence to support an explanation about how a factor affects biodiversity or a population. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can use math as evidence to explain how a factor affects a population or biodiversity.

column4: Revise an explanation about factors affecting biodiversity or populations when new mathematical evidence or data is presented. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can use new data to revise my explanation of what affects a population or biodiversity.

column4: Taught in Unit 4.2: Patterns in Populations.
Define carrying capacity and name factors that limit it, such as resources, space, climate, and competition. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can define carrying capacity and name what limits it.

column4: Read a population graph to find the carrying capacity and describe how the population changes as it approaches it. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can find carrying capacity on a graph and describe the population's growth toward it.

column4: Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of factors that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can use graphs and data to explain what sets an ecosystem's carrying capacity.

column4: Taught in Unit 4.2: Patterns in Populations.

Describe how complex interactions keep the numbers and types of organisms in an ecosystem fairly steady when conditions are stable. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can describe how an ecosystem's many interactions keep it steady.

column4: Distinguish modest changes, such as moderate hunting or a seasonal flood, from extreme changes, such as a volcanic eruption or sea level rise, by their effect on an ecosystem. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can tell a small disturbance from an extreme one by what it does to an ecosystem.

column4: Evaluate claims, evidence, and reasoning that the complex interactions in ecosystems maintain relatively consistent numbers and types of organisms in stable conditions, but changing conditions may result in a new ecosystem. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.2]
column5: I can judge the claim, evidence, and reasoning about whether an ecosystem stays stable or becomes a new one.

column4: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how the availability of natural resources, occurrence of natural hazards, and changes in climate have influenced human activity.
Identify the major types of natural resources, natural hazards, and climate factors that influence human populations. [DOK 1; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can name the resources, hazards, and climate factors that shape where people live.

column4: Describe how natural resources (fresh water, fertile soil, minerals, fossil fuels) are unevenly distributed across regions. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can describe how resources like water and fertile soil are spread unevenly.

column4: Describe examples of natural hazards (volcanic eruptions, earthquakes, tsunamis, floods, droughts) and how they affect where and how people live. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can describe how hazards like earthquakes and floods affect where and how people live.

column4: Explain how changes in climate (sea level, temperature and precipitation patterns, crop and livestock viability) can affect populations and drive migration. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can explain how climate change can move people and change what they grow.

column4: Interpret data, maps, or case studies that show relationships between Earth's resources, hazards, or climate and patterns of human activity. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can read maps and data that connect resources, hazards, or climate to human activity.

column4: Construct an explanation, based on evidence, for how the availability of natural resources, the occurrence of natural hazards, and changes in climate have influenced human activity. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can use evidence to explain how resources, hazards, and climate have shaped human activity.

column4: Taught in Unit 4.3: Earth Shaping Humanity.

Describe properties of water that change Earth materials: it expands when it freezes, dissolves many materials, and carries and drops sediment as it flows. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can describe the properties of water that let it break down and move rock and soil.

column4: Carry out an investigation of how water weathers, erodes, or deposits Earth materials, such as with a stream table, record the data, and connect the result to the rock cycle. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can carry out a test of how water wears away or moves Earth materials and record data.

column4: Plan and conduct an investigation of the properties of water and its effects on Earth materials and surface processes. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.3]
column5: I can plan and carry out my own investigation of water's effect on Earth materials.

column4: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution for reducing the impacts of human activities on the environment and biodiversity.
Identify and explain how human activities (e.g., pollution, deforestation, climate change) impact ecosystems and biodiversity. [DOK 2; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can explain how human activities like pollution and deforestation affect ecosystems and biodiversity.

column4: Create an evidence-based solution to reduce the negative effects of human activities on the environment and biodiversity. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can design a solution, based on evidence, that reduces a human impact on the environment.

column4: Assess the feasibility, benefits, and limitations of a solution aimed at reducing human impact on the environment. [DOK 3; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can judge whether a solution will work, and what it gains and costs.

column4: Use feedback and new evidence to improve a designed solution to mitigate human impacts. [DOK 4; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can use feedback and new evidence to improve my solution.

column4: Effectively communicate and defend a designed solution using scientific evidence and reasoning. [DOK 4; Priority (on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can present and defend my solution with evidence.

column4: Taught in Unit 4.4: Solutions for Sustainability.

Name Earth's systems (hydrosphere, atmosphere, cryosphere, geosphere, biosphere), with the cryosphere as the frozen part of the hydrosphere, and one way each connects to another. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can name Earth's systems, including the frozen cryosphere, and one link between two of them.

column4: Read the published output of a computational model, such as a graph or map, that shows how a human activity changes one Earth system. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can read a computer model's graph or map of how people change an Earth system.

column4: Use a computational representation to illustrate the relationships among Earth systems and how those relationships are being modified due to human activity. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can use a computer model's results to show how human activity changes links among Earth's systems.

column4: Taught in Unit 4.4: Solutions for Sustainability.

Describe data on a human impact, such as pollutant amounts, change in biomass and species diversity, or area of land converted. [DOK 1; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can describe data that measures a human impact on a natural system.

column4: Compare how well technological solutions, from local to large-scale, change that data. [DOK 2; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can compare how much different technologies reduce that impact.

column4: Evaluate or refine a technological solution that reduces impacts of human activities on natural systems. [DOK 3; Supporting (taught and practiced, not on the unit test); Unit 4.4]
column5: I can judge or improve a technology that reduces a human impact on nature.
